subject: obstetrics-gynaecology
title: Cell-Free Fetal DNA, NIPT and Chorionic Villus Sampling

steps.tx: Fragments of placental DNA circulating in maternal blood form **cell-free fetal DNA**. It derives mainly from trophoblast turnover, not the fetus directly. Levels rise with gestation and vanish within hours of delivery. A fetal fraction of at least 4 percent is needed, and most laboratories report failure below that threshold.
steps.say: Cell-free fetal DNA comes from placental fragments circulating in maternal blood.

steps.tx: A blood test on the mother reads placental DNA without touching the pregnancy. **Non invasive prenatal testing** counts chromosome fragments in cell free DNA and screens for the common trisomies with high sensitivity from ten weeks. It remains a screening test: a high chance result needs diagnostic confirmation before irreversible decisions. Low fetal fraction, vanishing twins and maternal chromosome variants explain many confusing reports.
steps.say: NIPT screens placental DNA fragments in maternal blood for common trisomies from ten weeks. High chance results still need diagnostic confirmation.

vis.alt: Image showing non invasive prenatal testing from a maternal blood sample.
vis.caption: A maternal blood tube is shown yielding placental DNA fragments for screening. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.tx: Screening maternal blood DNA for fetal chromosome imbalance is **NIPT**. Non invasive prenatal testing detects over ninety nine percent of Down syndrome with very few false positives. It remains a screening test needing invasive confirmation when positive. False positive rate for Down syndrome runs near 0.1 percent, far below the 5 percent of combined screening.
steps.say: NIPT screens blood DNA with very high Down detection but positives need confirmation.

vis.alt: Down syndrome screening context for NIPT.
vis.caption: NIPT screening context. [Credit: StewardMD]

steps.tx: Sampling placental villi for karyotype from eleven weeks is **chorionic villus sampling**. Transabdominal or transcervical routes both reach the placenta under ultrasound guidance. It gives earlier diagnosis than amniocentesis at slightly higher procedure risk. Sampling before 11 weeks raises failure and mosaicism problems, so 11 to 13 weeks is the usual window.
steps.say: Chorionic villus sampling takes placental tissue from eleven weeks for early karyotype.

steps.tx: Insufficient fetal DNA fraction causes test failure, reported as **no call result**. Obesity, early gestation and certain chromosome patterns lower the fraction. Redraw succeeds in most cases a week or two later. Failure itself slightly raises aneuploidy risk, so a no call result still earns a detailed scan offer.
steps.say: A no call result from low fetal fraction usually succeeds on redraw later.

steps.tx: Because the DNA is placental, confined placental mosaicism can mislead, a limitation called **placental origin error**. Rare false positives and negatives arise this way. This is the core reason positives need diagnostic confirmation. A positive result confined to the placenta can leave the fetus normal, which amniocentesis, not CVS, best clarifies.
steps.say: Placental origin means mosaicism can mislead NIPT, so positives need confirmation.

steps.tx: Sex chromosome and microdeletion panels extend testing beyond the main trisomies as **expanded panels**. Accuracy falls sharply for these rarer conditions. Many guidelines advise against routine microdeletion screening for this reason. Positive predictive value for a rare microdeletion can fall below 20 percent even with a good test.
steps.say: Expanded panels test rarer conditions with sharply lower accuracy and limited endorsement.

steps.tx: A twin who vanished early can keep answering blood tests for weeks. The **vanishing twin effect** leaves placental DNA from the lost twin circulating in the mother, so cell free DNA screening may report that twin genome instead of the survivor. Early scans documenting a second sac therefore change how results are read. Discordant screening results after a vanishing twin need diagnostic testing rather than anxious repetition of the same screen.
steps.say: A vanished twin placenta keeps shedding DNA that can distort screening results for weeks. Early scan documentation changes how those results are read.

vis.alt: Image showing a vanishing twin, one gestational sac resorbing beside a surviving twin.
vis.caption: Two early sacs are shown, one shrinking beside the surviving twin. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.tx: A vanishing twin can contaminate results with DNA from the demised co-twin, termed **vanishing twin effect**. The extra DNA persists for weeks after demise. Ultrasound before testing identifies this and other confounders. Ultrasound also dates the pregnancy, and testing before ten weeks is the commonest reason for a failed result.
steps.say: A vanishing twin leaves DNA that contaminates results for weeks after demise.

steps.tx: Couples declining invasive testing may still value NIPT for birth planning, a use termed **preparation value**. Knowing a diagnosis lets delivery and neonatal care be organised. Screening consent should explore this motivation sensitively. It can also determine fetal sex from ten weeks with accuracy above 99 percent where disclosure is lawful.
steps.say: NIPT can prepare birth and neonatal care even when invasive testing is declined.

steps.tx: Rapid targeted tests on villi or fluid give preliminary results in days, called **rapid aneuploidy testing**. Full karyotype or microarray follows for complete information. Counselling explains what each layer can and cannot detect. QF-PCR checks chromosomes 13, 18, 21 and the sex chromosomes, missing balanced rearrangements a karyotype would catch.
steps.say: Rapid aneuploidy testing gives early answers while full karyotype follows.
